Mamdani Administration Releases 40,000 More 9/11 Records to Public for First Time in 25 Years
articles.content: NEW YORK — Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and the New York City Law Department today announced the release of 40,000 additional City records related to the horrific terror attacks of September 11, making them available to the public for the first time in 25 years. Last month, Mayor Mamdani made history by creating the City’s first public portal for 9/11 records, nyc.gov/sept11docs, and settling a multiyear legal battle over air quality and health concerns following the attacks. For years, first responders, elected officials and families of victims of 9/11-related illnesses have demanded the release of these records. Mayor Mamdani’s FY27 budget includes $34 million to create and maintain the public records portal, which now features more than 200,000 pages of including the long-discussed Harding Memo and the materials known as the “68 Boxes.” “Our commitment to honoring the victims of the horrific terror attacks of September 11 and delivering accountability and transparency to survivors cannot begin or end on the anniversary. The first responders, family members and survivors of that terrible day deserve transparency and accountability from their City government every day,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “When we created the City’s first public records portal related to September 11th and released the first 170,000 pages, we made an enduring promise of documents, it wasn’t a box-check — it was the first of many steps we are taking to bring closure and clarity to millions of New Yorkers. I am proud to release these next 40,000 documents to the portal for the first time in New York City and looking forward to the work to come.” “For decades, families of 9/11 victims, 9/11 survivors, first responders and advocacy groups had to fight municipal bureaucracy to get the transparency they deserved,” said Corporation Counsel Steven Banks. “Today, we are expanding on our commitment by making tens of thousands of additional documents regarding the City’s response to September 11 available to the public.” “In the aftermath of September 11, New Yorkers were left in the dark about what City officials knew about the quality of the air we were breathing. 25 years later, and we are finally getting answers. Today’s announcement is an important step toward transparency and accountability, with the release of 40,000 documents that will help shed light on one of the darkest chapters in our city’s history. Thousands of New Yorkers suffered devastating, life-threatening health consequences from exposure to the toxic air, and our families deserve to know the truth. This release would not have been possible without the leadership of the New York City Council, Council Member Gale Brewer, and the many tireless advocates, and I thank the Mamdani Administration for their commitment to transparency and making this a reality,” said City Council Speaker Julie Menin. “What we have seen, after a review of the documents that have been released so far, is a disturbing record that even when the extent of the hazards were realized, the City, the State and the Federal government did not change course, slowing down the return of the community to homes, schools and offices, or at the least having a better cleanup effort,” said Benjamin Chevat, Executive Director of 911 Health Watch Inc. “Mayor Mamdani and Corporation Counsel Steve Banks continue to deserve credit for their agreement with 911 Health Watch to make these documents, that had been hidden for decades public—and for their commitment to releasing even in the coming months.” “For a quarter century, 9/11 survivors, first responders and the families of those suffering from 9/11-related illnesses have sought to know exactly what the City knew about air quality concerns around Ground Zero, and when they knew it. Today, the Mamdani administration takes another stride forward in its commitment to providing New Yorkers with the transparency they deserve. I commend the Mamdani administration for releasing 40,000 additional records to the public, and thank Mayor Mamdani and Corporation Counsel Steve Banks for their leadership,” said Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal. “Kudos to Mayor Mamdani and Corporation Counsel Steve Banks for living up to their commitment to release more 9/11 documents as they find, scan and post them to the publicly accessible portal,” said Council Member Gale A. Brewer. “I hope the revelations provide some measure of closure to those families who have been coping with 9/11-related illness or death—and serve as an example to future administrations how to manage a disaster with clarity and transparency rather than evasion and denial.” This release is the second installment of records being made public under the court agreement between 911 Health Watch and the Mamdani Administration. Additional records will be released in the coming months. New Yorkers can visit the September 11th documents portal at nyc.gov/sept11docs.

Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years behind bars
articles.description: Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years behind bars AP News Russia frees 74-year-old American Stephen Hubbard it captured in occupied Ukraine CNN American released from Russian custody lands at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland KSAT Retired American teacher imprisoned by Russia returns to U.S. NBC News Sister of American Stephen Hubbard says he’s in disbelief following release by Russia AP News
articles.content: Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top U.S. envoy and at a time when President Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow. Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the U.S. did not have to give up anyone in return. “He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man.” Hubbard’s legal team denied the Russian accusations, saying he was not involved in any military activity. The release occurred during a visit to St. Petersburg by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. AP correspondent Ed Donahue reports an American held in Russia is now free. Hubbard, who before his arrest had lived in Ukraine for years, was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison during closed court proceedings. Prosecutors said he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military after Russia’s invasion in 2022, and that he fought alongside Kyiv’s forces until being captured two months later. The U.S. government under President Joe Biden’s administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained. His family also disputed the Russian allegations. “He was just for bait. It was all about bait. And that’s why they kidnap Americans,” his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, said in an interview with The Associated Press. She said she expected Hubbard to stay with her in Colorado. “Steven James Hubbard is the face of America,” she said. “They could do that to anybody. They just happened to see him. ‘Oh, that’s an American, let’s go get him.’” Witkoff, a key Trump administration figure who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end a war that will hit the five-year mark in February 2027, thanked Putin for releasing Hubbard, telling him, “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.” “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was “raised by the American side for a certain time,” and Putin decided to free the man out of “humanitarian considerations.” Speaking to reporters after the talks, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the Kremlin leader had pardoned Hubbard, who upon his release was taken to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport for Witkoff to bring him home to the United States. Video showed Witkoff and Hubbard shaking hands, with the newly released American thanking the envoy. Witkoff introduced Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev to Hubbard and described him as someone “who had a lot to do with this happening.” “We just met President Putin, he sends you blessings and wishes you good things,” Witkoff added. Hubbard, a U.S. Air Force veteran, taught English overseas and had by 2012 retired to Cyprus, where one of his sons is a priest. He later moved to Ukraine to be with a woman he had met, his lawyers said, remaining in the country after the relationship ended and living there at the time of Russia’s 2022 invasion. He was detained in April of that year after Russian forces took control of the area where he was living. His case was taken up by lawyers at the U.S.-based law firm of Boies Schiller Flexner and the Russian firm of EPAM Law, which together had represented Marc Fogel, the American teacher freed from Russian custody last year, and worked for his release. “They thought they weren’t going to see him again alive, and Stephen didn’t think he was going to come out of there alive,” one of Hubbard’s lawyers at Boies Schiller, Martin De Luca, said in an interview of Hubbard’s family. “Obviously, they’re overjoyed, but they feel very much like it’s a miracle.” His sister said she had spoken with Hubbard soon after his release. “That was awesome. He was just laughing. He said, ‘I can’t believe this is happening,’” Hubbard Fox said of her brother. Trump told reporters Wednesday night that Hubbard is expected to visit the White House some time in the coming days. The release occurred at a dynamic moment in relations between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship being roiled by fresh tensions at the same time that the Trump administration has advanced policies that aid Putin. Those include Trump’s move last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after the late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Moscow’s war. That decision followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections. Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday. He was expected to exchange ideas from that meeting, as well as proposals from European and American colleagues, in his talks with Russian leaders in St. Petersburg. Hubbard is the second American freed by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of Marine veteran Robert Gilman, who had been gravely ill and was imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer. Other Americans, including some with serious illnesses, remain jailed in Russia. Hubbard was the last remaining American designated as wrongfully detained, although advocates say that label should be applied to other prisoners. When asked Wednesday night if he thinks more Americans will be released, Trump told reporters, “Yeah, I think so. That’ll come.” Russia reported more arrests of foreigners in recent days. The FSB security service said Wednesday it detained a German national suspected of mercenary activities and last week announced arrests of a Swedish national suspected of sabotage and a Japanese journalist accused of espionage. Associated Press writers Thomas Peipert and Michelle L. Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: Hackel: increased state funding will improve road conditions
articles.content: With Macomb County bolstered by an additional $150 million in upcoming state funding, County Executive Mark Hackel predicted the number of roads that are labeled as in “good or fair” condition under its jurisdiction will increase by 4% to 6% per year over the next five years. Hackel and Interim county Roads Director Scott Wanagat spoke at a “state of the roads” press conference Wednesday to highlight current and upcoming road improvements that are taking place over the next year or two with the help of an estimated increase of $150 million more dollars over five years from the state Neighborhood Roads Fund that was just over a year ago. Those dollars will be in addition to $474 million in funding it will receive under the traditional funding of Public Act 51, the Michigan Transportation Fund. That is a nearly 32% increase in state road dollars over the half-decade. “We’re going to start seeing an incremental increase in roads going to fair or good condition because of the work that’s going to be put into preservation but also into the new road fixes,” Hackel said. “We’re focused on making every dollar count, finding creative solutions and working with our local communities and state partners to keep Macomb County driving forward.” Of the 1,700 miles of county roads, 52.3% are in good condition and 47.7% are in poor condition, according to road officials. Those percentages are expected to increase to 61.7% of roads in good or fair condition and decline to 38.3% in poor condition in 2030, officials said. The Michigan County Roads Association recommends counties achieve a 60% rating of good or fair roads, according to Wanagat. The county is receiving $15 million in new funding under the NRF and $86 million in the traditional MTR funding this year and is projected to receive $26 million in new funding from the NRF and $94 million from the MTR fund. The remaining $109 million would come over the next three years. Hackel noted a caveat — the projections are “rough” estimates and “guess-timates.” “Our team is positioned to accelerate the progress we’ve made while maximizing every available dollar through strategic investments, creative engineering and comprehensive planning,” Wanagat said. “We know exactly how many assets we have, the condition they are in and how much it will cost to fix them properly.” The county is responsible for major roads throughout the county and local roads in townships, in partnership with the townships, the executive said. Cities and villages are responsible for their local roads and are receiving increased funding under the NRF plan, too. Hackel said county officials have been in talks with local officials on coordinating projects; a great deal of the funds will be spent on maintaining roads so they are in better condition and last longer before a reconstruction is needed. “I think we’re coming to an agreement on how we want to use that money,” Hackel said. “A lot of it is going to be specific toward preservation. Many of them (local officials) agree that if you’re going to fix a road, let’s maintain that road so it stays a good road for a longer period of time.” Hackel said there will be an increased emphasis on improving roads in subdivisions under the NTF program. “From the driveway to the highway, we’re working on those fixes,” Hackel said. “If we’re going to fix roads, the most important is the one out in front of your driveway.” The nearly $2 billion state-road financing plan over five years will be funded by: — $1 billion per fiscal year from a sales tax and motor fuel tax swap that began on Jan. 1, 2026; — $420 million of revenue generated from a tax on the marijuana industry; — $600 million by shifting from the Individual Income Tax to the Corporate Income Tax; and — $440 million from corporate income tax growth. “The local roads Michiganders drive on everyday are getting a major investment,” said state Sen. Veronica Klinefelt, D-Eastpointe. “We’re giving communities across Michigan the resources they need to transform their pothole ridden roads into safer, smoother paths for folks to get around — all while creating thousands of good-paying jobs along the way.” The county is spending $119 million this year when road construction and maintenance are combined with bridge work and traffic upgrades. The major projects that started and some finished this year include: – Mound Road resurfacing from Eight Mile Road to Interstate 696 in Warren at a $2.5 million cost to serve as a temporary fix to the crumbling road as the county seeks additional state funding for its $100-million reconstruction. The county has secured $8.5 million for the project so far. It a companion project to the more than $200 million reconstruction of Mound from I-696 to Hall Road (M-59), which was dubbed Innovate Mound and mostly completed in 2023. – Dequindre Road resurfacing between Eight Mile and one block north of Stephens Road, and between 13 Mile Road and 14 Mile Road in Warren at a $2.2-million cost. – Metropolitan Parkway resurfacing between Mound and Van Dyke Avenue in Sterling Heights. – Expansion of Broughton Road between 23-1/2 Mile Road and 24-1/2 Mile Road in partnership with Macomb Township to create a new downtown district in the township that includes work to accommodate pedestrians, roundabouts, new water main and sewer and culvert construction. The project broke ground last July and is anticipated to be completed next year. – Relocation of William P. Rosso Highway (M-59) at Harrison-Chesterfield townships border, which began in August, to accommodate a new, longer runway for a new fighter-jet mission consisting of 21 F-15EX fighter jets and accompanying KC-46A refueling tankers that are expected to arrive in late 2028. The $28-million project, which began in August, includes transforming a straight stretch of highway into a camel hump, creating a roundabout at Town Center Boulevard, relocating road drainage infrastructure, redirecting the Irwin Drain, and constructing concrete box culverts. The project is a partnership between Michigan Department of Military and Veterans Affairs, Selfridge Air National Guard Base and Macomb County. Officials pointed out a future project that is a high priority is rebuilding the Metropolitan Parkway bridge, which carries vehicles over an active railroad corridor, as the thoroughfare is a “critical link through Macomb County.” Officials are seeking additional funding for the project. Hackel said preservation work has been taking place at the bridge to extend its life, but that it will be in need of replacement in the near future. For next year, the Roads Department is planning to spend $99 million in infrastructure upgrades. Hackel said he is especially pleased that Joy Boulevard from Gratiot Avenue to Irwin Drive (at the Selfridge border) — which he called the worst in the county — will finally be rebuilt at a cost of $5.3 million following years of consideration among the entities of the county, and Harrison and Clinton townships. Other project to start next year include: – Schoenherr Road 23 Mile Road to 25 Mile Road in Shelby Township, $15.1-million reconstruction; – 21 Mile and Heydenreich roads intersection in Macomb Township, $7.4-million reconstruction and “rehabilitation”; – Jefferson Avenue from Rosso Highway to 23 Mile Road in Chesterfield Township, $6-million rehabilitation; – Garfield Road from Hall Road to 21 Mile in Macomb Township, $5-million reconstruction; – 10 Mile Road Hayes Road to Kelly Road in Eastpointe and Roseville, $4.8-million reconstruction and rehabilitation; – Harrington Street from Groesbeck Highway to Hilldale Street in Clinton Township, $3-million reconstruction; – North River Road bridge Over the Catfish Channel in Harrison Township, $5 million replacement; and – North Avenue bridge over the East Branch Coon Creek in Ray Township, $2.9-million replacement.

Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
articles.description: Just 9 months after raising a $180 million seed round, Flapping Airplanes has landed a $1 billion Series A for its mission to build AI models "without ingesting half the internet."
articles.content: Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation. The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled. Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company. Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT. Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn, a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it. The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.) The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.” The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched. They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.content: Meta had to shell out $9.89 billion to pay for a chunk of the child safety settlement it reached with US attorneys general. That’s according to the company’s third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, which says Meta’s income from operations would have been $22.89 billion without the settlement. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle a massive nationwide lawsuit that claimed the company harmed children by making its social media platforms “addictive” by design. It will also only pay $5.3 billion of this amount if YouTube and TikTok implement stricter settings and safeguards for kids, which Meta also agreed to as part of the settlement. Meta’s total costs and expenses amounted to $51.61 billion, including the amount it agreed to pay as part of the settlement. The company may have even bigger litigation costs in its future, as a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal on Wednesday. articles.title: Flying Roadsters can’t lift Tesla’s flat Q3 revenues
articles.description: As the smoke clears from its outrageous Roadster demo, Tesla reported Q3 earnings on Wednesday - and the cold reality is that revenue has flatlined. Tesla said it earned $1.7 billion in net income on $28.0 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended in September 2026. articles.content: As the smoke clears from its outrageous Roadster demo, Tesla reported Q3 earnings on Wednesday — and the cold reality is that revenue has flatlined. Tesla said it earned $1.7 billion in net income on $28.0 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended in September 2026. Revenues were flat, while profits dropped 4 percent compared to the third quarter of 2025, when the company earned $1.4 billion in net income on $28.1 billion in revenue. Tesla’s revenue came in above Wall Street expectations of $27.9 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Tesla’s own company-compiled expectations predicted Q3 revenues of $28.3 billion. The earnings come on the heels of a disappointing Q3 sales report, in which Tesla reported a 2.1 percent drop in customer deliveries compared to the blockbuster third quarter of 2025. (For a direct-to-consumer company like Tesla, deliveries are a proxy for sales.) The drop in sales was widely expected thanks to the expiration of the $7,500 federal tax credit for electric vehicles on September 30, 2025. Elon Musk himself said that the company was in for “a few rough quarters” thanks to the expiring incentive and other macroeconomic factors. Tesla reported automotive revenues of $20.5 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year — a sign that the company’s car business is floundering after the elimination of the tax credit. But there were troubling signs for Tesla’s other businesses too; the company reported $2.9 billion in energy generation and storage revenue, a staggering 16 percent drop year over year. “Services and other revenue,” such as money the company takes in from EV charging, maintenance, parts, and insurance, was up 33 percent to $4.6 billion – a rare bright spot in an otherwise dour earnings report. Tesla’s capital spending — also known as capex — soared 110 percent year over year to $4.7 billion this quarter, as the company continue to pour money into AI, autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Musk has said to expect “a massive capex year” of at least $25 billion in capital spending as Tesla continues to transition into an AI and robotics company. But the company only spent $13 billion in the first three quarters of the year, suggesting that Tesla may fall short of that $25 billion target. Operating expenses — the day to day costs of running Tesla’s business — was up 39 percent year over year to $4.8 billion, while its income from operations — the profit Tesla generates from those day-to-day dealings — was down 56 percent year over year to just $718 million. On the brighter side, Tesla reported a free cash flow of $1.5 billion, after dipping into negative territory last year. Still, that figure represents a 62 percent drop year over year, a sign that Tesla’s operating revenues were still struggling to cover its capital expenditures. The possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger gained new momentum after Musk’s revelation this week that the two companies had formed special committees to discuss the possibility. Musk said a merger would be a “good idea,” even though he claimed he wouldn’t be involved in the process. Beyond merger talks, this past quarter also saw the highly anticipated re-reveal of the next-generation Tesla Roadster, nine years after it was initially announced. The demo in Waco, Texas, featured a redesigned two-seat prototype flying and flipping through the air using cold-gas thrusters provided by SpaceX. While the event generated its own cottage industry of online reactions, it did little to assuage skeptics that the vehicle would actually go into production in 2028, as promised.

articles.title: Mamdani admin drops 40K more 9/11 health documents previously kept from public
articles.content: Firefighters are responding to the release of documents regarding air quality after 9/11. Lynda Baquero has more details. The Mamdani administration’s second document dump of 9/11 records is now complete. The cumulative 210,000 pages now posted on the city’s new 9/11 portal offer an unusual glimpse of discussions between city agencies and the lawyers representing them. Such communications — which would typically remain hidden under attorney-client privilege — are now being made public after the Mamdani administration waived that protection earlier this year. “When we created the City’s first public records portal related to September 11th and released the first 170,000 pages, we made an enduring promise of documents, it wasn’t a box-check – it was the first of many steps we are taking to bring closure and clarity to millions of New Yorkers," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday in a statement shared with NBC New York. Launched on Sept. 8, searches of the growing database continue to unearth efforts by the city to shield itself from lawsuits and potentially sweep health fears and World Trade Center dust under the rug. In December 2002, 15 months after the terror attacks, many Lower Manhattan buildings were still inundated with dust. At the time, according to an email exchange posted on the 9/11 portal, The City University of New York, Board of Elections, and other downtown residents were seeking decontamination help from FEMA. The EPA also indicated they would pay for specific building cleanups – if the city's Department of Environmental Protection certified those buildings as contaminated – according to emails on the portal. But in December 2002, the city's law department objected, telling DEP to "refrain from getting involved." Attorney Lawrence Khan, who worked the Law Department’s WTC unit, voiced concern that acknowledging hazardous conditions could subject the city to lawsuits since their previous position had been that the conditions were safe. “The Law Department is concerned that DEP certification that a facility is contaminated at a hazardous level will be used as evidence against the City in actions alleging that the City acted improperly in permitting continued occupancy or re-occupancy of the facility,” Khan said in the email. NBC New York was unable to immediately reach Lawrence Khan for comment. In response to an inquiry from News 4, longtime Bloomberg spokesman Stu Loeser declined to comment on any of the specific communications between members of the Bloomberg administration included in this story. A previous email chain from April 9, 2002 suggests confusion and poor communication about how to handle contaminated buildings. An environmental representative from Mayor Bloomberg’s Office expressed “surprise” that the EPA had told the city on April 8 that it had “believed all along” and “had said orally since Day 3” that indoor spaces with “more than minimal dust” should be professionally cleaned. The City, however, had not advised the public to professionally clean indoor spaces and it’s unclear why local officials were unaware of the EPA’s alleged guidance. A 2003 Inspector General report said EPA officials said they had consistently recommended that residents obtain professional cleaning during interviews, public forums and other communications since day 3 after 9/11. The IG noted the earliest example their investigation could find was on October 26, 2001, when then-EPA Administrator Christine Todd Whitman recommended professional cleaning in an interview on MSNBC. “Just wiping it down, using your regular vacuum cleaner, that’s not good enough. But you know, we provided that information and it is up to the City Health Department and OSHA and others to follow up,” Whitman said. In the Spring of 2002, Mayor Mike Bloomberg's office convened an interagency air quality task force. According to minutes documenting its first meeting in March 2002, the top lawyers at city agencies including the Department of Health, Environmental Protection, and others discussed air quality, building safety and public messaging. "We've been telling people everything is okay. We're just doing this to make people happy," then General Counsel of the Department of Health Wilfredo Lopez said, according to the notes posted on the portal. The notes also say that in the same meeting, Mark Hoffer, then General Counsel of NYC DEP, asked "How do we reconcile telling people they now have to do testing or clean up if we've been telling everyone things are OK?" A subsequent notation appears to describe the “general consensus” as “not contradictory” to redirect the public message after telling people “everything is OK,” but NBC New York’s efforts to glean clearer context from staffers who attended that meeting were not immediately successful. “Reading these documents, ordinarily privileged and protected, puts the reader ‘in the room’ with government officials and lawyers, as they spoke freely about the most significant event in New York City history,” said attorney Andy Carboy who represented 911 Health Watch Inc, the organization that sued the city for years to make these documents public. Benjamin Chevat, Executive Director of 911 Health Watch, added that the documents reviewed so far show “a disturbing record that even when the extent of the hazards were realized, the City, the State and the Federal government did not change course.” The portal was set up in September as part of a settlement of a multi-year legal fight over air quality, legal concerns and lack of transparency. “Kudos to Mayor Mamdani and Corporation Counsel Steve Banks for living up to their commitment,” said Upper West Side Council Member Gale Brewer. “I hope the revelations provide some measure of closure to those families who have been coping with 9/11 related illness or death.”

Macron slams as ‘stupid’ claims by Trump and others blaming Muslim migrants for French riots
articles.description: Macron slams as ‘stupid’ claims by Trump and others blaming Muslim migrants for French riots AP News France protests: Macron condemns 'stupid' comments from Trump, others as bond-market pressure builds CNBC Macron slams ‘stupid comments’ from world leaders after Trump blames France unrest on migrants CNN Some foreign leaders blame migration for France’s riots. Macron says that’s ‘stupid.’ The Washington Post France b
articles.content: PARIS (AP) — French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — were seeking to exploit France’s tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of street violence and looting. Protests over soaring living costs have led to widespread rioting and looting that have drawn worldwide attention and shocked many French citizens. U.S. President Donald Trump has used the violence to rally his political supporters, making unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest, and urging Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late!” Macron responded by saying there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other French cities last weekend. “And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” He added that there have been “AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.” Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said his office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, “to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media.” Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches. “The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country,” Macron said. “So those people really bother me.” “When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic — who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France — they’re using our country for their own political campaigns,” said Macron. “And we don’t need that.” Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in Gulf Arab states, where he secured an additional 100,000 metric tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tons to be confirmed in Bahrain. Macron’s office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel. The Élysée said nearly 295,000 additional tons of diesel per month could be secured, including supplies from Saudi Arabia — equivalent to more than 10% of France’s monthly diesel consumption. Macron later traveled to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman “to continue efforts to secure and diversify oil and gas supplies,” according to his office. Earlier this month, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products, beginning with substantial quantities of diesel after the fuel’s price hit a record high in the United States. “I would remind you that France initiated the G7 meeting that led to the release of strategic reserves, which, through implementation at the national level, will help bring down prices starting in early November,” Macron said. Petrol, energy and food prices have surged in recent months, and it remains to be seen whether Macron’s announcement will ease protesters’ anger. He said the additional diesel supplies addressed “some of the anxieties.” “I also hear the concerns of our high school and university students. Those concerns stem from other factors, but in any case, I think things are moving in the right direction,” he added. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also say school days, which often run from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., are exhausting and the university admissions system is complex and unfair. France has had two consecutive quiet nights since the weekend’s unrest. Curfews have been imposed in parts of several major cities, including small areas of Paris. Further protests are planned for Thursday and Saturday following calls from student unions and groups within the “ yellow vest ” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019. Paris police said Wednesday they would ban Thursday’s planned protest in the French capital, citing concerns for public safety and the protection of property. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures. “We are using the legal means at our disposal to prevent further incidents of this kind,” Macron said. “Those who intend to cause disturbances in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so. Tomorrow, we will also have a very detailed update on the implementation of these measures, including anticipation, intelligence gathering and security, not just for Saturday, but also for the coming weeks.”

articles.title: Mike Rogers, Abdul El-Sayed pitch competing economic visions
articles.description: In a break from personal attacks, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers talked policy in a Detroit Economic Club luncheon, covering tariffs, tax policy, artificial intelligence and more.
articles.content: DETROIT — Speaking to a crowd of Michigan business leaders, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers on Tuesday both advocated for a shift in approach to Canadian tariffs, though they diverged in their overall assessments of the Trump administration’s trade policy. Rogers made waves earlier this month when he called for an end to the “tariff war” with Canada, backing off his longtime defense of President Donald Trump’s tariff strategy. During a Detroit Economic Club forum on Tuesday, Rogers said he doesn’t think additional taxes on one of Michigan’s largest trading partners are helpful: “When they went to Canada, I thought that was not the right direction, and mainly because they didn’t account for how integrated we are in the automotive business,” he said. Trump first proposed broad tariffs on Canada in March 2025. He announced additional 50% tariffs on Canadian imports this summer, and those took effect in August after negotiations failed. Rogers did not immediately oppose the Canadian tariffs and on Tuesday said other Trump administration tariffs have had a positive impact, citing recent manufacturing reshoring by the automotive industry, some of it in Michigan. El-Sayed was more critical, arguing the federal strategy since Trump began his second term has been more about exerting power over other nations than it has about improving conditions for US workers. “I’m not against tariffs per se, I’m just against dumb tariffs,” El-Sayed said, calling the Trump administration tariff policy “chaotic,” “hamfisted” and “self-serving.” El-Sayed said he’d prefer to see a tariff approach that puts the US in a competitive position internationally, pitching the possibility of producing and subsidizing a low-cost electric vehicle that can compete with Chinese and Korean models while maintaining production of gas-powered engines. The two US Senate candidates were both given separate platforms to share their economic visions at the Tuesday event, a day before they’re set to meet for a second and final debate. El-Sayed billed himself as a capitalist who believes the United States is currently trapped in an oligopoly, arguing that his progressive platforms like Medicare for All, additional taxes on the wealthy and pro-labor policies would make the market more competitive and boost employers and employees alike. Pointing to Michigan’s lackluster rankings on education and economic opportunity, Rogers pitched a framework of boosting skilled trades, keeping taxes low and prioritizing US energy sources to begin bringing down costs while boosting opportunity. El-Sayed, whose campaign has released several policy proposals on artificial intelligence, said he’s concerned AI companies “are about to open Pandora’s box” when it comes to automating much of the job market, data safety and environmental concerns about data centers. He reiterated his calls for requiring a public ownership stake in AI companies, establishing a regulatory agency to oversee the development of AI models and expanding the list of banned AI activity. Rogers said AI platforms “definitely need guardrails” and said establishing a national framework for AI regulation would be a top priority for him if elected. Rogers also said he supports a “narrowly crafted” exemption to antitrust laws to allow AI companies to collaborate on safety measures. Both candidates agreed that impediments to affordable housing were hampering economic growth and preventing people from moving to or staying in Michigan. “I want to be a destination for future talent, I don’t just want to be a place that barely holds on to the kids that we grow here,” El-Sayed said, calling for down payment assistance programs and building “competitive hubs” of housing around small businesses to stimulate growth. Rogers expanded on his campaign’s housing agenda, which involves loosening regulations, using land banks to address vacant lots, creating tax-free construction zones to encourage building in certain markets and adding the option of tax-free savings accounts for first-time homebuyers Improving Michigan’s education system and increasing access to skilled trade training in schools would also go a long way toward improving Michigan’s economic stature, Rogers argued, calling skilled trades “a job China can’t steal, and … a job AI can’t replace.” El-Sayed called for pro-labor legislation to “enable union organizing in every sector of American life,” arguing that doing so would better enable labor organizations to work in concert with the small business community. He also supports cutting the payroll tax and investing more in small business growth. “Fighting for unions and also fighting for small businesses allows us to make sure that we’re building and creating and maneuvering more wealth in and around our communities, so that more people have more of the pie,” he said. Rogers told the business-friendly audience that he supports a lower tax rate for businesses to give them room to invest, while also bringing more certainty to the market. He said he supports tax credits for research and development but argued the Green New Deal, which El-Sayed previously supported, would have required “the largest tax increase in the history of the country.” El-Sayed used the forum to advocate for one of his signature policy platforms: taxing the wealthy, which he argued could be a good way to tackle the country’s debt burden and combat trends of cutting taxes for the richest while raising costs for others. “Anytime somebody like me steps up and says, ‘I actually think we can have health care and good schools,’ they’re like… ‘What are we going to do about the national debt?,” he said. “I don’t know. Maybe stop fighting wars we shouldn’t be fighting, and maybe we should tax the richest people.” To do so would unlock “a lot of the latent economic opportunity that does not actually get manifested,” he said. “Right now we’re in a system where if you’re winning, you are absolutely winning. Nobody else gets the money.” This article first appeared on Bridge Michigan and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. articles.title: Election 2026: Still need to register to vote? Here’s what to do.
articles.description: As of Oct. 20, 2026, if you still need to register to vote, you must do it at Detroit City Clerk’s Office.
articles.content: As of Oct. 20, 2026, if you still need to register to vote, you must do it at Detroit City Clerk’s Office, 2 Woodward Ave. #200 Detroit, MI 48226. Here’s what to do. First, verify if you are already registered by putting your information into https://mvic.sos.state.mi.us/Voter/Index and it will tell you. You need the following qualifications to vote: You can register to vote at the Detroit City Clerk’s office Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The office will have special hours the weekend before the election. You need to prove that you live at your address, so you must bring a printed record of one of the following: Want to vote before Election Day? You can vote in person at the Detroit City Clerk’s office or at an Early Voting Site starting nine days before Election Day. When you vote at an Early Voting Site, your voting experience will be similar to that of voting at a polling place on Election Day. You will complete your ballot, place it in a secrecy sleeve and then deposit it into the voting tabulator. Note: Some drop box locations are at the buildings listed. Some are located elsewhere in the parks or campuses. The addreses will take you to the correct locations. Want to vote in person on Election Day? You must vote at your assigned polling place. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. If you are in line by 8 p.m. at your polling place, you will be able to vote. You can find your polling place online at the Michigan Voter Information Center or by calling the Detroit City Clerk at (313) 224-3270. Your polling place will likely be near the address you registered to vote with. But it may have changed from last year, so verify before you show up to the polling place. If you encounter what you believe to be misinformation, you can report it to the state by emailing misinformation@michigan.gov. Read more about how to be an informed voter and detect misinformation.
